rationale: The title and abstract clearly address urban household/community water access and equity outcomes in water-deprived areas of Nairobi (Criteria 1 and 4 met). Full-text retrieval is required ('unsure') for two reasons: (1) under the narrow Criterion 2 reading, examining Nairobi Metropolitan Services, changes in the city's overall governance structure, and pandemic water projects plausibly involves administrative/institutional restructuring, utility-governance rules, or emergency tariff/free-water mandates, though it could also be generic project delivery; and (2) the abstract does not explicitly state its empirical methodology (Criterion 3 unclear).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under literal/plain Criterion 2, the study clearly examines institutional and urban water governance changes (Nairobi Metropolitan Services and city governance restructuring), whereas under the narrow rule-type reading it is unclear from the abstract whether specific legal, administrative, regulatory, tariff/subsidy, or utility-structure rules are analysed rather than generic government water project delivery. Both readings yield 'unsure' at Title/Abstract because full text is also needed to verify empirical methods (Criterion 3).

evidence_quotes.quote: Covid-19 and Nairobi Metropolitan Services as Co-Catalysts of Waterscape Changes
In our paper, we focus on changes in urban (water) governance and government water projects in Nairobi since early 2020.
However, if these waterscape changes lead to greater equity in water access, and if they have helped to curb the spread of SARS-CoV-2, is more than questionable.
